speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bertrand (Laurier) for the second reading of Bill No. 28, to amend the criminal code.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because I am convinced, after careful consideration of the proposal to legalize sweepstakes for the alleged purpose of assisting hospitals and universities, that the appeal has nothing to commend it from any point of view, on either economic, political or moral grounds. On the contrary I regard it as utterly and completely fallacious by every test of logic and by the proof of historical fact. Of course, I do not for one moment question the good intentions of the hon. member who has moved the bill (Mr. Bertrand, Laurier), but I would remind him of the well known adage that the road to perdition is paved with good intentions.
The hon. member refers to the fact that some years ago in Vancouver a majority of persons voted in favour of a plebiscite which involved the idea of sweepstakes. Surely the hon. member does not suggest for a moment that the fact that a majority of the electors in Vancouver voted in favour of this idea was an endorsation of the principle, because I am unable to see any principle in it.
May I suggest to the hon. member another reason which these people had for voting

Criminal Code-k^jepstakes
for the idea of sweepstakes. The hon. member knows as do all hon. members of the house, that the majority of the people of this country are very poor. They live constantly in the shadow of a terror that clutches at their hearts, the fear of how to pay for rent and food and clothes and education for their children, and they often go to bed haunted by terrible nightmares of penniless old age, and those nightmares which concern young men and young women wandering hopelessly through the streets and roads of the country in a fruitless search for work,- those nightmares concerned with sickness and death without anyone to provide for their children.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
We have
very often been told that we are living in a happy country, and I always thought so myself.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
I should like to agree with the hon. member that we are living in a very happy country, but the evidence before me as I go through this country tells me another story altogether, and I am just telling that story as I see it.
I suggest that this proposal, like most of the shallow and superficial thinking which characterizes our present day leadership, is an attempt to rearrange the consequences of the deep-seated ills which afflict society rather than to discover and remove the causes. Men and women of all races and colours and creeds, as I have found them in my experience in the commercial life of Canada for twenty-five years, are naturally kind and good and decent, and it is contrary to the deepest instincts of humanity to want something for nothing or to live parasitieally off the labours of others. It is by their institutions alone that people become corrupt, and the responsibility for shaping and ordering these institutions nearer to the heart desires of humanity rests heavily upon the leaders of men. But if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
I suggest that the people of Vancouver voted for lotteries, not because they favoured the principle, because there is no principle, but because they live constantly in the shadow of the terror of poverty. What normal human being, living under conditions of heartsick, bitter poverty and frustration, does not long for that happy dream-world of freedom, security and contentment which the sudden possession of great wealth seems to offer. It matters not that, according to the most authentic figures which I have been able to gather, only one in three thousand ever receives a prize. Always in his dreams and prayers is the fond hope and longing that he may be that one.
But if the prize does come to such a lucky one, what of the other three thousand whose hopes can never be realized and whose dreams can never come true. If the prize winner has a reflective mind, he will soon realize that his suddenly acquired fortune has not been gained by either honesty, industry, thrift, or any virtue whatsoever; nor has he contributed a single thing to the community by way of the creation of useful or consumable new wealth or services. The whole thing has been accomplished by an intensification and a deepening of the poverty, deprivation and suffering of others. Often the last pathetic pennies of the desperately poor, pennies sorely needed for milk, bread and other bare necessities of helpless little children, are taken and used in a desperate gamble to get something for nothing. Then the prize winner becomes the most complete embodiment of the cruelty, injustice and utter lack of morality of a system under which decent human beings are compelled to fight each other like wild beasts in the jungle because of the false and pernicious teaching, or other teachings like it, that "competition is the life of trade" and that they must compete and strive with each other for things which may be had in abundance without competition. This individual is automatically vested with privilege and power, backed by the respectability and sanctity of law and order, so-called, and at once, despite the untenable nature of his position on any grounds of ethics, morality or common decency, is able to lord it over the lives and destinies of his unfortunate neighbours, whom he can now command to feed, elothe, entertain and protect him and his descendants forever, or as long as the interest system lasts, without their having to render a single useful service in return. I say, Mr. Speaker, it is every one of these manifold contradictions, cruelties, infamies and horrors that this bill seeks to uphold, to condone and to perpetuate.
The hon. member has made reference to another unfortunate method of raising funds for public purposes which is even more degrading and demoralizing than sweepstakes. I refer to the liquor traffic. It has been stated that Ontario's liquor bill last year was $72,000,000. Ontario has about one-third of the population of Canada. It is therefore safe to assume that the people of Canada spent about $200,000,000 on booze last year and that the various provincial governments would get about $40,000,000 out of that. But what an awful price to pay, when it is realized that all that people get in return is something which injures both body and mind, as Shakespeare says, "putting a thief into the mouth
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

to steal away the brain!" They get more than that. They get ghastly slaughter on the highways, the undermining of health and morals, financial ruin, and a heavily increased demand on the hospitals and morgues of the country. Think, Mr. Speaker, of the irony of the suggestion that organized gambling and booze could by any stretch of the imagination assist in the operation of hospitals! Is it not organized gambling, not only in sweepstakes, but through stock exchanges, in the necessities of life, which drives thousands of people in this country into hospitals, mental institutions, gaols, and premature gra%res, and is this not equally true of booze? How many of the poor people who would gamble their last dollar on a sweepstake to help a university, ever would or could have the privilege of a university education? And besides, what is the use of turning out graduates from high schools and universities when there are such limited opportunities for employment?
Then, Mr. Speaker, think of the shocking waste involved in this method of raising money. We have heard that even the Irish people are protesting against the Irish sweepstakes because of the injury inflicted upon their hospitals; but even apart from that, according to Mr. C. E. Silcox, writing in the New Outlook of April 8, this year, out of a total of three hundred and twenty-five million dollars paid into the twenty Irish sweepstakes up to March, 1937, only about fifty million has found its way into the coffers of the hospitals, or just 16 per cent, which means that the expense of raising this money was 84 per cent, while some community chests have been able to reduce their costs of collection to less than 10 per cent of the amount collected.
Any state that legalizes lotteries will have a new source of income-I dp not question that -but must also be prepared for the consequences, and these are some of them. It will gain a few thousands of dollars at a cost of millions to its people. It will increase its own relief problem. It will encourage new rackets and racketeers. It will not be able to frown upon other forms of gambling. It will do incalculable harm to the morals of its children and its adult irresponsibles. It will increase public disrespect for governments. The contention that our hospitals would benefit, the plea that much money is now going out of the country on foreign sweepstakes that might as well be kept at home, to me are utterly fallacious-devil's arguments in defence of a racket that, from beginning to end, seethes with duplicity and dishonesty.
(Mr. P. J. Rowe.]
During the past three years-and I do not want to be left constantly in a negative position; I want to be able to offer something as an alternative to this-I have stated in this chamber many times that there is a living in sound goods and services of more than 84,400 a year for every family in this country, enough to place every person beyond the borders of poverty and want forever, enough to provide comfortable homes, freedom, security and the happiness that everyone is seeking, if only sound and scientific principles of producing and distributing the wealth that we have and our resources were adopted. There is no possible excuse or reason for their not being adopted. With that income, we would have not the slightest difficulty in keeping up our hospitals and universities. The average man with a salary of $4,400 has no difficulty whatever in making a reasonable contribution and paying adequate taxes to maintain these institutions.
The cure for the present loss or shortage of money in the pockets of the people can be found only by removing the cause. This is not a cure; this is an attempt to rearrange the consequences rather than to examine and remove the cause. I say we would be able, if we would undertake scientific and rational methods of producing our wealth and distributing it equitably, to do so without having to resort to such shameful, degrading and criminal methods as dishonest gambling and poison booze. I have repeatedly asked this government, and I again do so now, to make a survey similar to the Loeb survey in the United States, of the natural resources, inventions and machinery on the farms and in the factories of this country, with a view to determining the potential product capacity of the country, not in meaningless gold, silver or paper dollars, but in consumable sound goods and services, and then, having determined what wealth could be produced, and thus the standard of living available to all the people, go on the radio and carry to every home and hamlet in the land the glad tidings of abundance. I know of sixteen ways by which money is now being made in this country, all of which are unmoral, unethical, injurious and inimical to the general welfare of the people, but all of which are nevertheless clothed with the sanctity of law. Let the government, after telling the people what these abuses are, announce its intention of removing them by passing laws to make them illegal, in order that the people may inherit the earth and its riches, to the mutual benefit of all, and the injury of none.

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
I do not intend to delay the house with any laboured argument of this question; but I do desire to make my position clear in a few words, and I shall refer to one or two arguments that have been advanced in support of the bill. I am opposed to this measure, which seeks to legalize sweepstakes in Canada, because I consider it uneconomic, anti-social and the most extravagant method yet devised for raising money for legitimate and, as indicated by some of the sponsors, desirable ends and purposes. It has been argued that it is justifiable to amend the criminal code to legalize sweepstakes for the purpose of raising funds for the assistance of hospitals and universities.
The law dealing with gambling as it stands in the criminal code is either a good law or a bad law. Either it is a law which it has been found desirable, from the experience of years, and, indeed, of centuries, to have on the statute books, or else a ghastly mistake has been made in maintaining it on the statute books and it ought to be removed. There is no more justification for having sweepstakes to assist a university or a hospital than there is for having sweepstakes for any other purpose that might be desired. The point is not what money or portion of the money obtained will be used for the purpose in question; the point is that gambling has been recognized as a dangerous social practice which ought to be curbed and kept in restraint. That is the experience.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Why are
there so many exceptions in the code?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
I have no objection to a person holding the view that gambling is a desirable thing and that the law against it is bad. Such a person is at perfect liberty to advocate that view. But I take my position very strongly on this ground, that this part of the criminal code has been maintained where it is because the majority of the people of this country, and indeed of many other countries, regard such a provision as in the interests of the social integrity of the nation.
The next point is this: It has been suggested that people are just dying to buy a sweepstake ticket so that they can help a hospital or a university. My hon. friend almost wept a week or two ago when he introduced the bill, when he gave us a picture of people in Montreal, Toronto and other cities looking eagerly for an opportunity to give their $2.50, or whatever the ticket may cost, for the purpose of helping some hospital, suggesting that we who opposed it were
preventing these Charitably inclined people from contributing their $2.50. If they want to contribute $2.50, why can they not simply stick it in an envelope with a three cent stamp and send it to the hospital? My hon. friend knows, and his smiling face shows that he knows very well, that these tickets are bought because people have an expectancy of a large winning with very little risk and at very little cost. It is the expectancy of a large winning. We know that; why camouflage the thing?
Again, it is a self-destructive method, because the more sweepstakes you have, the less any one of them can benefit. One of the reasons why the Dublin sweepstake attracts such a huge amount of money is that it is one of the few large sweepstakes in the world and therefore it draws from the world. There are many people in Canada and in the United States who buy tickets, and a part of their money goes over there-we do not know how much reaches Dublin but some of it does-why? Because the sweepstake draws from the whole world. But if you had a sweepstake in every province in Canada, you would simply restrict the field from which winnings could be drawn.	.
The people who buy tickets in the Dublin sweepstakes, with the huge prizes that are offered, will still buy them although they might support one in Montreal or Toronto or Vancouver or some other place. I contend, however, that it is a self-destructive method. The more it is permitted and the more it extends, the less profitable or useful it will be. It is an extravagant method, moreover; that has been demonstrated. I shall not trouble the house with figures; they are available to anyone who wishes to study them. As the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Rowe) has pointed out, about 16 per cent of the huge sums that have rolled into Dublin, with all the glamour and fascination of that sweepstake. has gone into the hospitals. I say, it is an extremely costly method.
The bill naively makes this proviso:
Provided there shall not be held more than one sweepstake. . . .
That is a limitation which has no justification. If this system of raising money is good; if it is sound; if it is justifiable, it ought not to be limited to any one hospital or to two or three favoured hospitals once a year. It should be something open to any institution. But the sponsors know perfectly well that if you multiply sweepstakes, you destroy the whole structure, and therefore it is very cleverly suggested that there should be one a year.
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

Another suggestion was made that a million dollars went from Toronto to Ireland and that this money ought to have been kept in Canada and directed into the coffers of Canadian sweepstakes. It was advanced as an argument that the people of Toronto-I do not know whether the figures are correct; I am simply taking the argument as advanced-who sent a million dollars to Dublin were so anxious to give it to a hospital that when they could not give it to a Toronto hospital they had to send it to a similar institution in Dublin. Therefore it was contended that we in Canada ought at once to give them an opportunity to contribute to a Toronto or an Ontario hospital. The argument has only to be stated to see how ridiculous it is. In the first place, if we had an Ontario sweepstake, people would still, if they could, buy tickets for the Dublin sweepstake. Why? Because of the hope of those $100,000 winnings. When the newspapers at each drawing for the Irish sweepstake spread the news of a family in New York, or Toronto or some other part of Canada, drawing $100,000, $125,000, $70,000, $10,000, and so on, the avaricious instincts of thousands of people are stirred up and they go out and buy a ticket-what for? To contribute to the Irish hospitals? No. They have no more interest in the Irish hospitals than that inkwell on my desk. All they are thinking of is that they have a wild chance of getting a winning ticket, which chance I understand, taking all the prizes together, amounts to about one in three thousand; something extremely small in any case
For these reasons and many others I am opposed to this bill. I repeat what I said just now, that the law against gambling as it appears on the statute books of this country is either a good law or a bad law. If the law is faulty we should correct it, not for sweepstakes for one purpose; for if sweepstakes are good for that purpose they are good for other purposes. That is not the test of the value of the law. The test of its value is that if it is desirable that some people should have an advantage, the same advantage ought (to be open to any citizen of Canada for any purpose. So I say the law is either good or bad, and the test should be whether we wish to remove from the statute books the law against gambling or whether we prefer to stand by the experience of a great many years and retain this law which most of us believe is necessary in the interest of good social conditions in this country.

speechtext:
After serious consideration I have decided to support this bill, not because I believe that the particular bill is necessary to prevent gambling or anything of that kind, bu't because I believe there should be a certain measure of control in this matter, as there is in other ventures in this dominion. Let me state briefly some of the reasons why I believe we Should have this control. Consider first the Winnipeg grain exchange, where speculation is permitted in the buying and selling of grain futures, not for the benefit of (the people as a whole but for the express purpose of making money. I refer to the grain commission inquiry report, page 47. In regard to speculation in grain futures, we find it said that:
. . . business on the Chicago board of trade would be seriously handicapped, if not wholly dislocated, by the elimination of speculative buying and selling (or even by the elimination of only speculative selling) in the market.
I am convinced by the evidence that the presence of speculators in the Winnipeg futures market is just as essential to the proper functioning of that market as is the case in Chicago. The volume of their transactions may not be as great and on this point there is no definite evidence, but experience has shown that in Winnipeg if the speculator is away the market is in difficulties.
And on page 48:
As long as you have the present method of marketing, speculation is a very necessary element in the existing system and its absence is certainly to be regretted.
I have no brief for gambling in any manner, shape or form; but in the case of the Winnipeg grain exchange, where we are permitted to endanger even the lives of primary producers through the manipulation of the market because of rising and falling prices, we also know that the percentage of winners is small. But as the profits made from this source assist the large grain brokers in handling the crop, assuring them of safe margins, the casino is permitted to exist.
We have the same conditions in the stock market. Stocks are bought mostly for the purpose of making money, not for the purpose of developing property or for any material interest in the welfare of the country. I have here a magazine, the Newsweek, dated May 30, 1938, in which I find the following item in reference to the stock market. It is rather amusing to me, after reading articles during recent months trying to explain why investors have not been taking advantage of the present low prices of stocks. I maintain that the reason is very simple; they have

Supply-National Health
been evading the discussion of the true reason. This article seems to cover the situation. It says:
Investment trust scandal.
Watch for a Wall street explosion with repercussions that may rival those of the Whitney scandal. It will come when the SEC and New York district attorney's office reveal results of an inquiry into three important investment trusts. Investigators have found that the three companies, whose securities are widely held by the general public, have been looted of their choicest assets. Revelations will show that manipulators managed to obtain control of the trusts by purchasing their depressed shares. They then replaced the former management, sold most of the valuable assets of the companies, and used the proceeds to buy shares of little known companies owned by the insiders.

In connection with health education I cannot but think back to what happened this afternoon when another item concerning food standards was under discussion. Elour shall be the fine, clean, sound product-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I cannot but admire the ingenuity with which the hon. member brings us back to an item which was passed in his absence.
Mr. WOODSW'ORTH: I admit that, but I related the subject to the item under discussion.
Mr. POW'ER: I shall not take advantage of the fact that the other item passed; I am not in the habit of doing that. The point is that under regulations made under authority of the minister, as conferred upon me by the Food and Drugs Act, there were certain regulations giving a description of flour. Flour was described as has been stated by the hon. member.
For many years a number of improvers, including potassium bromate, have been tolerated. Some one in the department issued instructions to some of the flour millers to the effect that potassium bromate would no longer be tolerated. One flour miller who apparently had not been in touch with the department wrote to me to find 
out the state of the case. I had an inquiry made, as I have a right to do under the authority conferred upon me as a minister. As a result of the inquiry and of investigations by the Department of Trade and Commerce, investigations by the Department of Agriculture and the opinion I was able to get from medical men, I came to the conclusion that the small quantity of potassium bromate which would be mixed in the flour in process of milling was not deleterious to humans. In order to get even the ordinary dose of potassium bromate which is usual in sickness, a man would have to eat a hundred loaves of bread.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My right hon. friend raises the point as to whether or not this is what I might call a continuous process of poisoning; that may not be the technical term.
Cumulative.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have left my papers upstairs, but I believe I can state the situation in non-technical terms. According to the opinion of Mr. Aitken of the grain board there is no such cumulative effect. I have that opinion in writing. After lengthy inquiry the British government came to the conclusion there were no deleterious effects; but, as I said this afternoon, the French government held a contrary view. The United States millers use potassium bromate, and they are in competition with us at every quarter of the globe. In certain sections of the world, and, I am told, particularly in hot climates, this substance has a beneficial effect upon the bread. What the process is, I am unable to say.
Moreover, so far as I am aware, there is nothing in any regulations which prevents a baker from using this substance indiscriminately, except that the bread may be seized when it is adulterated, or made dangerous for human consumption. So that it appeared to me, after listening to the representations made and from all the information I could get, that there was no reason why this should not be permitted. In consequence of that, the regulations which strictly defined what should be flour have been deleted. But that does not lessen in any way the protection given to the public under the Food and Drugs Act. Prosecutions may be instituted just as before if there is any adulterant used in the flour. In so far as the public are concerned, they have just as much protection as they had before. In regard to the technical question as to whether or not potassium bromate is deleterious, in the exercise of the authority conferred upon me

Supply-National Health
as minister, after listening to all the evidence that was tendered, I came to the conclusion that it was not. However, I do not say that I am infallible.

tolerate it for the time being, at least.

At the same time, I do not think his explanation is altogether satisfactory. Apparently the millers are determined to have this substance in the flour in order that they can export. The former provision was quite clear. The regulation read:
3. Flour shall be the fine, clean, sound product made by bolting wheat meal, and shall contain not more than thirteen and five-tenths (13-5) per cent of moisture, not less than one and twenty-five hundredths (1 - 25) per cent of organic nitrogen, nor more than two (2) parts per million of nitrite reacting nitrogen, not more than one (1) per cent of ash, and not more than fifty hundredths (0-50) per cent of fibre.
There is a similar regulation with regard to bleached flour. Those regulations were specific and definite and the millers were held responsible for upholding that standard. But there is no standard to-day. They have asked that these regulations be deleted in order that they may use this one particular substance, potassium bromate, as an improver.

They can introduce a dozen things that they call improvers, and there is nothing to safeguard the public.

This is a complete reversal of the previous procedure. Under the former regulations the millers were held responsible, and now some one must prove the product deleterious.

speechtext: We have full authority under section 4 of the Food and Drugs Act.
What evidence is required? I suppose some one will have to be poisoned and then there will be an investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The public would be protected in this case as it is in connection with sausages or hamburgers or all those things.

The explanation given by the minister is perfectly clear and straightforward, and should be grasped easily even by the lay mind. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) appears to be making a mountain out of a mole-hill. Potassium bromate is not a 
deleterious or injurious drug at any time. It has no cumulative effects, and if it is used in the process of baking as an improver for yeast this is done only with the idea of promoting the chemical action which goes on in the process of bread-making. It has been put forward here as an argument against its use that those who are engaged in the trade and handle flour are subject to skin eruptions and other diseases because of the use of potassium bromate. That I may say, broadly speaking, is not the case. There are individuals who are susceptible even to the action of flour on their hands and arms. They have what we call an idiosyncrasy for that type of thing, and it has never been proven that the addition of potassium bromate as an improver of yeast in the making of bread has one iota of effect in producing skin eruptions. If our export flour to hotter climates particularly, Jamaica and the West Indies, demands the addition* of an improver of the type of potassium bromate, that is doing nobody any harm, and we are simply adding to the flour something which will help to sell it in those particular countries. Its use even in our own country for domestic purposes does not do one iota of harm.

The statement of the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) is most reassuring, but it does not meet the point we have been endeavouring to make this afternoon and this evening. Standards were formerly prescribed, but the door is now more or less wide open to doubtful practices. The minister intimated that the Maple Leaf Milling Company were content to proceed with the processing of their flour without the use of potassium bromate.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Either the Maple Leaf Milling Company or the Lake of the Woods Milling Company. I have not my papers before me at the moment.

Does that not lead to the conclusion that the same results might be achieved in the quality of bread by the more careful processing of grains, without the use of questionable substances? Certainly, I think we should make a stand against the use of any form of adulterant or improver, if it is possible to process satisfactory and wholesome flour without it. Bread is an article that goes on every table, and it is vitally important that the strictest regulations should exist to protect the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Every baker has been able to use potassium bromate for years almost ad lib, and he can do so yet. It struck me at the time that it would be preferable, if it were desirable to permit the infusion of this

substance, to have it done scientifically by the miller, to simply throwing the substance in, in handfuls, in a bake shop. I thought it better to control it scientifically, rather than have it done in a haphazard fashion.

Item agreed to.
Industrial hygiene, $11,450.
Would the minister give a detailed description of just how industry benefits from this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have a memorandum here on the subject:
The purpose of industrial hygiene is to develop methods for the protection and improvement of the health of industrial workers. It has now become an integral part of any public health program dealing with the prevention of disease.
Comprehensive surveys in many countries and states have shown that illness and injury in industry have increased in direct proportion to the widespread use of hazardous processes and injurious materials in an ever increasing variety of industrial uses. Moreover, un-healtbful industrial environment not only causes specific occupational diseases but increases the incidence of tuberculosis, pneumonia and degenerative diseases (heart, kidneys, nervousness) among workers. As the result of increased health hazards and lowered health standards of workers, there have developed serious economic problems.
The first step undertaken by the division of industrial hygiene has been the creation of a technical advisory committee on industrial hygiene.
In that connection we called into consultation representatives of the Department of
Labour, representatives of all the provinces, representatives of the universities and of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, also university professors, as well as representatives of organized labour. We called them in to help us to elaborate a program.
The duties of the committee will be to institute studies in respect of industrial diseases and hazards associated with special industries with a view to determining the problems presented in this field and the methods that may be adopted for their control. Where indicated, special methods that have as their object the reduction of industrial disease hazards will be investigated.
The division of industrial hygiene will conduct special studies regarding illness in industries in cooperation with provincial departments of health. The division will disseminate to the provincial departments of health and to industrial concerns scientific knowledge in respect of industrial diseases gleaned from world-wide research and experience gained in the matter of reducing health hazards in industry.
An endeavour will be made by the division to encourage industrial establishments to adopt a uniform morbidity code, which has been developed by this department in order that sound comparisons may be made with regard to illnesses in various industries. The provinces will be encouraged to take a greater interest in industrial diseases and, where possible, to establish divisions of industrial hygiene. Efforts will be directed towards the development of uniform legislation in regard to sanitation of industrial establishments with the object of obtaining equitable and uniform standards for the provinces and control of industrial diseases throughout the country.
It is believed that as a result of the activities of this division measures may be adopted to reduce working hazards in industry generally.

Is not all that now
taken care of by the provincial departments of health, and if so, is not this department merely supplementing or assisting in some way in the work the provincial departments are doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The work is really collecting information and making studies which will be of some use to the provinces. At the present time three provincial governments have branches of industrial hygiene-Ontario, Quebec, and, I think, Manitoba; but it is possible, by research work and studies of what is going on in other countries, that we may be able to obtain for the provinces information which will be very helpful to them. It is not intended that we should go into industrial establishments and undertake their supervision, by putting into effect factory laws oi regulations for the prevention of accidents. It is rather the study of occupational diseases, which workmen's compensation boards have had neither the time nor the opportunity to
Supply-National Health

study. I must say that Ontario has made more progress perhaps than any country in the world with respect to silicosis, and it will not need our assistance in that regard.

The discoveries made
by the department are simply passed over to provincial departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous grants-Grant to the Canadian Welfare Council, $8,100.

I notice that the grant
to the Canadian Welfare Council this year is $8,100, but the grant last year and for a number of years was in the neighbourhood of $13,100. I should like to pay tribute to the council as one of the voluntary agencies in this country which has been carrying on public health work. The fact that the grant is not as large as it has been in previous years is not because the organization is doing any less work or less important work, but there has been established in the department a public health branch which will take up maternal and child welfare and thus relieve the council of some of the work it has been doing for the public health of the dominion. I believe that in paying tribute to the Canadian Welfare Council I voice the sentiments of those who are engaged in health work in Canada and of those hon. members who are interested in public health activities. I agree that the right policy is being followed by the reestablishment within the department of a division of maternal and child welfare which will gradually take on the work that was formerly done by the department and which for the last number of years has been done by the Canadian Welfare Council.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
L Association Canadienne Francaise ties Aveugles, $4,050.

What particular work is
being done by this institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This is the French-Canadian association for the blind.
Is the institution indicated in item No. 249 an association for the blind?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It also is an institution for the blind.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Montreal Association for the Blind, $4,050.

Why the grant for the Canadian National Institute for the blind

and the special grant to the Montreal association? Is not the Montreal association connected with the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They do not seem to work together. They have never done so. I do not know which has seniority, but (they both do very good work in their separate fields. I believe the Montreal institution for the blind was founded by a Mr. Layton-probably the hon. member remembers him-who has been prominent in working for the blind and particularly in pressing for pensions for them. For some reason or another this association has never coordinated its efforts with those of the Canadian National Institute.
Is there any overlapping?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think so. I think the Montreal institution looks after the English speaking blind in the province of Quebec, and there is some kind of agreement that, so to speak, one will keep out of the other's territory. I do not believe there is anybody outside the province of Quebec who belongs to the Montreal institution.

May I ask how
many people, are treated or helped?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not know that I can give the hon. member the number. I can tell him what work is being done. This association operates a school for the blind and an industrial home in Montreal. Its activities include a boarding school for the blind and partly blind boys and girls, a workshop for blind men, a workshop for blind women, a boarding home for blind men,, a residence for blind women. It has a lending library of over 2,000 volumes in braille, a home teaching and social service department; glasses are distributed free to needy patients; there are pensions and money allowances, food, coal and clothing; and social activities which are attended by blind people from all over the city. We have given the same amount each year since 1927.
The minister has no information with regard to the numbers?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; I have not it here.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grant to the Canadian Red Cross Society,

This grant to the Canadian Red Cross society is 810,000. I notice that the grant to the Victorian Order of Nurses is $13,100. Why should the grant to the Red Cross be less than the other?

Supply-National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I really do not know, but the answer I am given is that the Red Cross society has been in existence the shorter time, and probably it has not got accustomed to getting any more. I will say this, that the Canadian Red Cross society would like to get a larger grant, and I should like to give it to them if I could.

I believe that is just as frank a statement as I have ever heard a minister make in this chamber. I notice that the Canadian Red Cross society is putting on an intensive campaign for funds, and its work is well known to everybody. I think the minister should very favourably consider any application on its part for an increased grant. It is doing wonderful work, and its organization is probably as large as that of the Victorian Order of Nurses. If the Red Cross society applies to the minister for an increased grant, I would appeal to him to give it favourable consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I make speeches in favour of their having more funds, but I am very sorry to say that I have not been able to get them any more. They are entitled to it; I have no objection to saying that.
How many outpost hospitals have the Canadian Red Cross?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Roughly, forty. I have not here all the details of the work of the Canadian Red Cross, but they do excellent work in their outpost hospitals and in many other places.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grant to the Canadian Dental Hygiene Council, $2,500.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why this increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is increased as a result of representations made in this committee last year that the &750 then granted was a ridiculous amount to vote. I agree.
What work does this organization perform?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It organizes surveys and puts on campaigns in the different provinces to look into the care of the teeth mostly of school children, but of adults also. It goes from province to province and carries on the work generally throughout the year, but every year or so it takes on a campaign in one particular province, in the way of dental health education, at the request of the provincial department. It does exceedingly good work.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Pensions branch-Pensions and other benefits -Pensions payable to men on active service, Northwest rebellion, 1885, and general pensions, $20,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Some representations were made that some of those who participated in the rebellion of 1885 had been overlooked, and there was communication with the department. Have their difficulties been adjusted?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My only recollection is that certain veterans of 1885 made representations that they also should come under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. They probably thought this was a new form of pension, because it is evident that anyone who served in the rebellion of 1885 and is now indigent would come under old age pensions.
Are the men who receive small pensions under this item entitled to unemployment assistance if they require it?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think we have ever had an application. I think we could arrange it, because the regulations with respect to unemployment assistance are pretty wide and it might be possible to look after them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Services to veterans and dependents-Care of patients, $3,045,287.

When we were discussing hospitalization last night I was going to ask the minister some questions regarding orthopaedic appliances. Are all those who suffer from pre-enlistment disabilities aggravated by war service entitled to such appliances?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Any appliance that has to be used or worn on account of a disability incurred or aggravated on service is given to the applicant.

Quite a number of men have complained, and on investigation of some of these cases there was a doubt as to their eligibility for assistance in this form. I have on my file a copy of a letter from the director of medical services indicating that appliances could not be given to men whose disability was aggravated during service.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
If the hon. member will
inform me of one case, I shall have it adjusted. Certain abuses of that kind have crept in, and if he will show me a service aggravated case where a man needs an appliance he will get it. He will get it whether the case is aggravated or incurred on service.

A number of men who
formerly, for quite a number of years, received special boots from the department
Supply-National Health

have had the issue of boots discontinued, and I am at a loss to understand why they should be denied that assistance. If a man has any actual disability which through the years has necessitated his wearing a special boot, and if he is not now provided with such boots and is unable out of his own resources to secure them-because they are fairly expensive, being specially made-the very loss of that form of assistance constituted a disability. I have in mind special cases of men who are making an effort to remain at wrork, and they are carrying on with difficulty because they no longer receive these special boots.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I understand that in some
cases orthopaedic boots would not always be needed. A man's condition may have so improved by the use of a boot that he would not need a second or third or fourth supply as the case may be. I understand that in 1932 or 1933 there was a review of all these cases, and there was perhaps a certain shrinkage in the number of those receiving boots. I would point out in the first place that there is no departmental policy that an aggravated case is not entitled to boots. In the second place, any of the cases brought to my attention where the free issue has been curtailed owing to the tightening up of rules and regulations in 1932 and 1933 have been attended to, and some way has been found of having the issue made; that is, when the consultant says that boots are necessary. I would not give a man a pair simply because he said he wanted them, because they cost $13 or $14.

With reference to men
awarded pensions under section 21 of the Pension Act, for compassionate or meritorious reasons, are they entitled to medical treatment as class one patients, on the same basis as other pensioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No. Under the regulations it would appear that treatment is given only for disability incurred or aggravated on service. Section 21 provides for the man who cannot get a pension under the pension law. Up to the present I do not know of any case where treatment has been refused, but the regulations have never covered it. Again, however, I say to my hon. friend that if he knows of a real case where a man who had service in France needs treatment and has not the means of obtaining it, I shall see that he gets it.

On a former occasion the
minister gave the names of the staff employed in the pension department at Shaugh-nessy military hospital, Vancouver. Can he
(Mr. MacNeil.]
give the staff so far as medical treatment is concerned? I am referring to the medical staff, and also the number of consultations.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The names are: G. C. Derby, the district administrator; Dr. J. H. Jones, Dr. F. H. Mahood, Dr. J. S. McCallum; Dr. J. Brown; Dr. A. B. Schinbein; Dr. W. A. Wilson; Dr. C. S. McKee; Dr. G. Draeseke; Dr. W. W. Kennedy; Dr. H. H. McIntosh; Dr. A. A. McRae.

Are any of those on the
permanent staff permitted to engage in private medical practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: All the part-time officers are on the permanent staff, in that they are permanent civil employees; but if my hon. friend means full-time employees, to my knowledge they do not carry on private practice.

I assume that this amount of $3,045,287 is for the medical care of the returned men. I really am at a loss to understand why, twenty years after the close of the war, it should cost so much for the hospitalization of those who were engaged in the war and who need the care of medical men. Everybody understands that it is costly to maintain hospitals, and I give way to no man in my desire to see the returned men well looked after. We are maintaining eight hospitals in Canada for returned soldiers. An investigation ought to be made with a view to establishing homes for these men. They could be as well looked after in returned soldiers' homes as in up to date hospitals with permanent, full-time officials and a full staff. If we are at the present time spending over $3,000,000 a year, twenty years after the close of the war, we have made no progress in that time in the method of caring for these men. We could well afford to have homes for them where they would be assured of all the comforts they would have if they were in good circumstances in their own homes. These institutions could be supervised by competent officials, and these returned men could have visiting, part-time medical services, and be just as well off at perhaps half the cost. I would recommend that the government give serious consideration to revamping the whole system of taking care of returned men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have heard this same proposal made by others, including one association of returned men, who said they thought that by this time we should give up our departmental hospitals and place all soldier patients in civilian hospitals. But I do not believe the cost would be much if any less

Supply-National Health
than under the present system. I put the suggestion to other returned soldier associations; I discussed it informally with the members of an association at a convention, and I was told it would not be popular with the soldiers to place ex-soldier patients in civilian hospitals. In the hospitals under the department they have the comradeship of their own friends; they have returned soldier doctors, nurses and orderlies; they are treated as a class by themselves. I do not believe it would please the ex-soldiers if I were to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend, although I admit it was strongly pressed upon me by a returned soldiers' organization, so he is by no means alone in his view.

Is it not true that practically all those now in the hospitals are there solely for the purpose of actual remedial treatment,
as determined by departmental medical authorities, pursuant to P.C. 91?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not quite all. Not half.
Is there any substantial number in the hospitals merely because they require domiciliary care?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The number is 378, to be exact, and my hon. friend must remember that we have a number of mental cases.
How many veterans, both in-patients and out-patients, received treatment in these departmental hospitals during the last fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The number runs from 2,300 to 2,500 every day in the year. I do not think it went over 2,500. It goes up in the winter and down in the summer.

The figures given in the report of the department, page 27, show 2,212 in-patients and eight out-patients, or a total of 2,220, as at March 31, 1937. Was there a smaller or a larger number on March 31, 1938?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think there is a difference of about 100. In 1937 there were 2,220; in 1938, 2,105. These consist of the three major classifications: general treatment, tubercular, and mental. I have not the total here; we have to add those in other hospitals, provincial mental hospitals. In British Columbia I believe there are about ninety-eight; they would not be included in this figure. And there are some in Saskatchewan.

In view of the fact that the numbers are decreasing, yet we still have the hospitals and the staffs, would it not be 51952-211
possible to extend hospital treatment to men who are not pensioners, although they have gunshot wounds, and also to recipients of the war veterans' allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: A large number of these are being taken care of now.
But some provision could be made for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not want to make any regulations which would restrict any chance I may have of doing this. I prefer to carry on as we have been doing and allow as many as possible in under the present regulations. I think we are doing that fairly successfully.
Has the minister the figures for the last few years showing the number of admissions and cost of care of patients and of hospital allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is in the annual report every year, but not yet available for this year.
How do your costs compare with civil institutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are lower than the average for civilian institutions. It does not cost us any more to look after our own patients than it would to put them in civilian hospitals.
Is it not a fact that there are many in these hospitals who are not under treatment but who are there more for the purpose of having a home?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes; 378 of them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous grants-Grant to the Association des Medecins de Langue Francaise de L'Amerique du Nord, $5,000.
For how many years has this grant been made to this association?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They do not meet every year; it is about every second year.
How many times has a grant been given to this association?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I know they had it about 1934 and 1936. I cannot say whether they had it in 1932.

What is the purpose of this grant, and what services are these people performing?
Supply

National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This is a conference of the French speaking doctors of North America. As a matter of fact, this year they are using the money, as I think they did on a former occasion, to 'bring distinguished medical men from the old country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: From Paris.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They brought someone from Paris on the last occasion, and I know it is their intention to do so this year. Whether it is one doctor or more, I cannot say. My hon. friend probably knows that a large proportion of the French-Canadian doctors and French speaking doctors throughout America received their education in Paris, and in order to keep in touch with medical knowledge over there and apply it in their work they found it essential to form an association of their own and to bring -people over who would keep them in touch with the latest developments.
At what place is the convention to be held this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It was in Ottawa the last time; this year I think it is to be in Montreal, but I cannot say for certain.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
